title: PACE: Geometry-Aware Bridge Transport for Single-Cell Trajectory Inference
abstract: Single-cell trajectory inference from destructive time-course snapshots is fundamentally ill-posed: neither cross-time cell correspondences nor continuous trajectories are observed, so the snapshot distributions alone do not uniquely determine the underlying dynamics. Existing optimal transport and flow-based methods typically couple cells by Euclidean proximity at observed clock times, which can misalign trajectories when development is asynchronous and cells sampled at the same experimental time occupy different latent pseudotime stages. We propose PACE, a trajectory inference framework that recovers geometry-consistent continuous transport dynamics from destructive time-course snapshots through three coupled components. First, PACE constructs a state- and time-dependent anisotropic Riemannian metric that assigns low transport cost along locally supported tangent directions while penalizing normal velocity components. Second, it alternates between refining cross-time couplings under the induced path-action cost and fitting endpoint-preserving neural bridges between adjacent snapshots. Third, it distills the learned bridge dynamics into a global continuous-time velocity field over cellular states. Across seven controlled and biological datasets covering nine held-out reconstruction experiments, PACE achieves the strongest overall reconstruction performance, reducing MMD, Wasserstein-1 distance, and Wasserstein-2 distance by 23.7% on average relative to the strongest competing baseline. PACE also improves RNA-velocity alignment by 15.4% on an embryoid body differentiation benchmark, without requiring explicit cell pairing, lineage tracing, or RNA-velocity supervision during training. Code is available at https://github.com/AI4Science-WestlakeU/PACE.

title: Diffusion MRI protocol design for reliable parameter recovery: a unified framework across biophysical models
abstract: Reliable microstructural parameter estimation in diffusion MRI (dMRI) critically depends on the acquisition protocol. Yet, common protocol design criteria may not fully reflect estimator bias, parameter constraints, and nonlinear fitting behavior in complex inverse problems. Here, we introduce Protocol Optimization via Loss Assessing Parameter Recovery (POLAR), an end-to-end framework that searches the continuous acquisition space and directly minimizes multiparameter recovery error through noisy signal simulation and the chosen model fitting. We demonstrate POLAR spanning distinct microstructural environments: the Cylinder-Zeppelin model for white matter, Neurite Exchange Imaging (NEXI) for gray matter, and Cellular Exchange Imaging (CEXI) for permeable cells. Across independent held-out parameter sets, POLAR consistently outperformed model-specific reference designs, reducing RMSE by up to $50\%$ for Cylinder-Zeppelin and $74\%$ for CEXI, while reducing NEXI exchange time bias by $70\%$. These gains across distinct biophysical models, acquisition settings, and reference design strategies demonstrate the benefit of optimizing acquisition protocols through the downstream parameter-estimation problem. POLAR provides a flexible, model-specific and estimator-aware framework for designing dMRI protocols tailored to the microstructural parameters and experimental conditions of interest.

title: Statistical inference for a multiscale stochastic model of enzyme kinetics via propagation of chaos
abstract: We study a class of Stochastic Differential Equations (SDEs) with jumps modeling multistage Michaelis--Menten enzyme kinetics, in which a substrate is sequentially transformed into a product via a cascade of intermediate complexes. These networks are typically high-dimensional and exhibit multiscale behavior with a strong coupling between different components, posing substantial analytical and computational challenges. In particular, the problem of statistical inference of reaction rates is significantly difficult and becomes even more intricate when direct observations of system states are unavailable and only a random sample of product formation times is observed. We address this problem in two stages. First, in a suitable scaling regime consistent with the Quasi-Steady State Approximation (QSSA), we rigorously establish a stochastic averaging principle yielding a reduced model for the product-substrate dynamics. Guided by the reduced-order dynamics, we next construct a novel Interacting Particle System (IPS) that approximates the product-substrate process at the particle level. This IPS plays a pivotal role in the inference methodology, and we prove several non-asymptotic bounds and limiting results for this system. These results facilitate the construction of an estimator based on a product-form approximate likelihood requiring only a random sample of product formation times. This approach does not need access to the system states, and we rigorously prove consistency of the estimator.
comment: Accepted for publication in the Stochastic Processes and their Applications

title: System-evolutionary view of RNA presence in living cells
abstract: Our guiding question for this article was: How did RNA adjust its life when the RNA world era came to an end? RNA has its practical execution side in the whole-cell systems setup serving critical functions in metabolism, compartmentalization, and in the RNA-DNA-Protein network, coupling information handling and different events of macromolecule production into a self-sustaining loop. Aligning with current views of cooperation we find that RNA life is distributed across a population of information-bearing entities persisting by compatibility, with DNA serving as a long-term memory and proteins offering the catalytic reach. We suggest that the reproduction-survival axis, relevant to higher organisms, is also manifested by RNA in many forms, including RNA-primers, mRNAs, tRNAs, and rRNAs. Each of these have contrasting, highly adapted molecular phenotypes. Ultimately, we wish to emphasize the evolutionary narrative where RNA did not lose in exchange for DNA genes or otherwise. Ultimately, RNA just changed strategy and in its various forms has an active and critically important presence in all cells at all times.

title: Curriculum-Augmented GFlowNets For mRNA Sequence Generation
abstract: We develop an approach for the de novo synthesis of messenger RNA (mRNA) sequences encoding target proteins. This requires optimizing multiple biological objectives over large combinatorial spaces defined by synonymous codon sequences, a setting where Reinforcement Learning (RL) methods suffer from mode collapse and Generative Flow Networks (GFlowNets) face sparse rewards over long horizons. To address these challenges, we propose Curriculum-Augmented GFlowNets (CAGFNs), a multi-objective GFlowNet trained with an adaptive length-based curriculum driven by learning progress. In a nutshell, CAGFNs learn from progressively harder tasks corresponding to longer target proteins. We evaluate CAGFNs on CodonDesignEnv, a novel codon-level environment that preserves protein identity via dynamic action masking. Our experiments show that CAGFNs achieve competitive or stronger Pareto-front coverage and diversity while converging up to 4 times faster than non-curriculum GFlowNets, and maintaining 100% sequence uniqueness compared to RL baselines.

title: Data-Driven Soft Labeling Scales DNA Read Classification to Whole-Body Cell-Type Deconvolution
abstract: Cell-type deconvolution, the task of estimating the proportions of constituent cell types in a heterogeneous biological sample, is a core problem in computational biology. Methods that rely on epigenetic marks such as DNA methylation typically operate on aggregated methylation estimates, discarding the pattern-level information carried by individual DNA reads. Existing read-level approaches that exploit this information are scarce, and all remain restricted to few-class settings; scaling them further is an open problem because, at scale, non-discriminative reads dominate and hard labels conflict with the many-to-many mapping between methylation patterns and cell types, preventing classifier convergence. To overcome this, we propose data-driven soft labels that estimate the conditional cell-type distribution for each read, and integrate this scheme into $Syto$, a new modular framework for read-level classification-based deconvolution. On a whole-body atlas of 39 human cell types, $Syto$ reduces MSE by 3.7$\times$ over the best examined baseline, with gains transferring to an out-of-distribution dataset spanning 16 tissues. $Syto$ lays the foundation for modeling increasingly large cell-type panels, with improved applications in biology and healthcare. The proposed soft-labeling scheme is further translatable to any setting with a many-to-many signal-to-label mapping.

title: BARRR: Bidimensional Augmented Reduced Rank Regression for Multi-View Multi-Cohort Data
abstract: Bidimensional data integration across multiple cohorts (i.e., sample groups) and views (i.e., sources or modalities) is crucial in biomedical research to derive holistic insights from heterogeneous datasets. However, most existing integrative methods focus on a single dimension, such as multi-view integration across distinct sources or multi-cohort integration across distinct sample groups. Existing approaches for bidimensional integration are scarce and predominantly unsupervised, overlooking the valuable insights offered by covariates. To address this gap, we introduce the Bidimensional Augmented Reduced Rank Regression (baRRR) method. Our approach models covariate-related and unrelated effects concurrently, while also decomposing effect levels (global, partially shared, and individual) across both dimensions. Extensive simulations demonstrate the advantages of our method with respect to signal recovery, outcome prediction, and missing data imputation. We apply our approach to data from The Cancer Genome Atlas (TCGA), using somatic mutations as covariates to inform patterns of variability across different omics platforms and cancer types. These studies highlight its potential as a robust and adaptable tool for integrative analysis in biomedical research.

title: Harnessing Magnitude-Only and Complex Measurements for Improved Dynamic MRI Reconstruction with Learned Priors
abstract: MRI reconstruction methods for undersampled k-space data naturally utilize complex-valued measurements. Parallel developments in sparse phase retrieval have shown that magnitude-only measurements may provide complementary information for signal recovery. However, their use in MRI reconstruction remains largely unexplored, due to lack of practical settings where informative magnitude measurements can be obtained without additional scan time. In this work, we investigate the use of auxiliary k-space magnitude information for accelerated steady-state dynamic MRI reconstruction, and demonstrate strong consistency of k-space magnitudes across time-frames. Building on this observation, we propose $\mathbb{C}+\text{Mag}$, a magnitude-informed physics-driven deep learning reconstruction method. The proposed method employs an ADMM-based unrolling framework with a novel magnitude-aware data-fidelity formulation, where quadratically smoothed optimization and momentum-based updates are introduced to address the non-differentiability and non-convexity of the magnitude constraints. Experiments on retrospectively undersampled cine MRI and phase-contrast flow MRI datasets, as well as prospectively undersampled real-time cine MRI acquisitions, demonstrate improved artifact suppression, sharper anatomical recovery, and better preservation of phase information compared to conventional PD-DL methods, which is further supported through blinded expert reader evaluations.

title: Determination of the Human-Robot Interaction Workspace for Robot Assisted Head Stabilization Control
abstract: Accurate head immobilization is critical for medical procedures such as neuroimaging and intracranial radiation therapy, where even minor motion can compromise precision. Traditional methods, such as rigid stereotactic frames and thermoplastic face masks, are invasive, uncomfortable for patients, and require a time-consuming setup. To overcome these limitations, a novel approach employs a 6-degree-of-freedom (6DoF) robotic head holder that is integrated with real-time optical motion tracking, enabling dynamic compensation for head movements without physical restraint. However, implementing this system requires a detailed biomechanical understanding of skull-cervical spine interactions to define safe and effective motion limits. In this study, we conduct a human volunteer investigation using a 6DoF Stewart platform robot to characterize biokinematic workspace of the head-neck system and establish foundational data for human-robot interaction in precision head stabilization.

title: EMBER: Predicting TCR--pMHC Binding Without a Docked Complex
abstract: We propose EMBER, a structure-based framework for TCR--pMHC binding prediction that eliminates the need for a predicted docked complex, and with it the placement error that dominates such predictions. Traditional structure-based predictors utilize the co-folded complex structure of the receptor and the antigen and interpret binding from its contact surface. Consequently, every downstream feature inherits any deviation the structure-prediction tool introduced. Methodologically, EMBER folds the TCR and pMHC independently, encodes them as SE(3)-invariant residue graphs, and compares their learned representations without constructing a shared coordinate frame. A relative pose is therefore not an input of the model, so placement error cannot propagate into the prediction. Computationally, EMBER preprocesses $O(N{+}M)$ monomer folds where a complex-based predictor needs $O(NM)$ operations. Experimentally, under epitope-disjoint evaluation with six retrained baselines, EMBER is first on every metric under all four folding tools, by 0.9 to 14.4% in micro-AUROC, 18.5 to 25.3% in micro-AUPRC and 10.6 to 24.1% in MCC. Its ranking is also up to 85% more stable across folding tools.

title: Reading Between the Reads: A Decade On, Revisiting Sequencing Protocol Annotation in the Sequence Read Archive
abstract: Background: Experimental metadata are essential for interpreting archived sequencing data. In 2015, Alnasir and Shanahan examined the annotation of fragmentation, adapter ligation and enrichment in the Sequence Read Archive (SRA). This study revisits those measurements using the original SQL keyword definitions on a September 2026 NCBI metadata snapshot reconstructed in the historical SRAdb schema. Results: The contemporary database contained 41,593,302 experiments, compared with 419,620 in 2013. In library_construction_protocol, the proportion matching all three historical keyword groups declined from 4.06% to 1.42%. The protocol field was NULL in 67.65% of contemporary experiments. Searching design_description alongside the protocol field increased combined three-step keyword detection to 1,197,367 experiments (2.88%), with most additional matches occurring where the protocol field was NULL. Coverage varied across sequencing library strategies, ranging from 0.26% for AMPLICON to 7.69% for RNA-Seq. Independent comparison of 150 sampled experiment records against source XML confirmed agreement in all historical keyword classifications. Conclusions: The original criteria identify a smaller proportion of experiments in the designated protocol field than a decade earlier. Additional preparation-related terminology is detectable in general experiment descriptions, exposing the limitations of searches restricted to one metadata field. Differences among sequencing strategies complicate historical comparisons as preparation methods evolve. The findings support more consistent protocol annotation and the need to distinguish keyword occurrence from the adequacy of experimental documentation.

title: Magnolia: A Persistent-Memory Agent Framework for Computational Chemistry
abstract: Chemistry has recently entered a high-data regime as molecular databases from high-throughput platforms or computational studies have become available. Increasing automation within the chemical sciences leads to a more digital and precision chemistry. Dedicated scientific agents are becoming central to guiding the chemist through an ever-increasing amount of data and findings, including negative ones. Here, we introduce Magnolia, a persistent-memory artificial intelligence agent framework that integrates computational protocols, from docking to quantum chemistry, lab notebooks and chat logs relying on large language models (LLMs). It relies on a three-tier memory system: session-level observations are automatically captured and distilled into structured learnings, confirmed and elevated to project-tier entries and, when human-validated, promoted to cross-project rules that actively guide subsequent work and provide direct chemical feedback. We illustrate Magnolia on four case studies: quantum-chemical evaluation of aromatic systems (COMPAS database), molecular dynamics of butane and of modified DNA, and a protein-peptide docking campaign. Across these projects, Magnolia tracked 317 runs and accumulated 116 project-tier entries, from which four cross-project rules were promoted; in controlled replays of four tasks, runs with memory passed the checks that runs without it failed (for example, ten of ten docking-configuration checks, against one to four of ten). By combining automation, reproducibility, and human-in-the-loop control, our Magnolia framework streamlines docking, molecular dynamics and quantum chemistry calculations with direct analysis and LLM-augmented feedback, offering accelerated access to computational (bio)chemistry.

title: Testing for genetic interactions in complex disease with distance correlation
abstract: Understanding epistasis (genetic interaction) may shed some light on the genomic basis of common diseases, including disorders of maximum interest due to their high socioeconomic burden, like schizophrenia. Distance correlation is an association measure that characterizes general statistical independence between random variables, not only the linear one. Here, we propose distance correlation as a novel tool for the detection of epistasis from case-control data of single-nucleotide polymorphisms. On the methodological side, we highlight the derivation of the explicit asymptotic null distribution of the test statistic. We show that this is the only way to obtain enough computational speed for the method to be used in practice, in a scenario where the resampling techniques found in the literature are impractical. Our simulations show satisfactory calibration of significance, as well as comparable or better power than existing methodology. We conclude with the application of our technique to a schizophrenia genetics dataset, obtaining biologically sound insights.

title: MoSAIK: Motion Search with Artificial Intelligence in K-space
abstract: Object: Motion artefacts remain a major limitation of routine two-dimensional T2-weighted turbo spin-echo (TSE) brain MRI, reducing diagnostic confidence and often necessitating repeated acquisitions. MoSAIK (Motion Search with AI in K-space) retrospectively estimates in-plane rigid-body motion directly from standard multi-coil TSE k-space. Without a motion-free reference, external navigators, or additional acquisitions, MoSAIK infers motion from k-space self-consistency violations and incorporates predicted parameters into model-based, motion-aware reconstruction rather than synthesizing corrected images. Materials and Methods: Selected complex coil data were represented as log-magnitude and phase channels. A decoupled convolutional embedding and Transformer encoder estimated phase-encoding-line-indexed rotation and two-dimensional translations. Training used motion-free clinical acquisitions with simulated motion; four held-out subjects were evaluated. Component-wise errors assessed estimation; SSIM and PSNR in silico and entropy focus criterion (EFC) in vivo assessed reconstruction. Results: Motion estimation errors were low for both rotation (MSE $<$ 0.2 deg$^2$) and translation (MSE $<$ 0.2 pixels$^2$), with Pearson correlations of approximately 0.96 and 0.94, respectively. In every in-vivo acquisition, more than 75% of slices showed information gain relative to uncorrected reconstructions. MoSAIK reduced visible artefacts while preserving anatomical detail. Discussion: Transformer-based k-space motion-trajectory estimation enables fast retrospective correction of standard clinical TSE brain MRI.

title: Cross-disorder Learning of Imaging-derived Joint Mophometric Markers in Alzheimer's and Parkinson's Diseases
abstract: As two most prevalent neurodegenerative diseases (NDDs), Alzheimer's disease (AD) and Parkinson's disease (PD) shared commonalities both in symptomology and pathophysiology. However, to what extent and in what way these two distinct disorders overlap remain underexplored. In this study, we propose an explicit, interpretable and spatially adaptive transfer learning framework to elucidate the morphometric biomarkers linked to AD and PD. We applied such high-dimensional machine learning model to two most popular open-source neuroimaging datasets, i.e., Alzheimer's Disease Neuroimaging Initiative (ADNI) and Parkinson's Progression Markers Initiative (PPMI). On the one hand, our cross-disorder classifier revealed neuro-anatomical alteration patterns well aligning with previous neuroimaging research findings and underscoring patients' clinical presentations. On the other hand, the spatially adaptive trained classifier using shared prior achieved statistically superior diagnostic performance compared to respective individual models, which further highlights the cross-disorder framework's efficacy on modeling limited-size datasets across disease domains.

title: ProteinGeoBench: Frontier Structural-Biology Agents Are Fluent at Lookup but Lost in Geometry
abstract: Frontier agents retrieve structural metadata well and compute geometry from coordinates less reliably. We ask how much of a benchmark score reflects that gap and how much reflects the evaluation configuration around the model. We study ProteinGeoBench, a suite of 131 protein-structure tasks, using 4,249 rollouts from four frontier models and 4,486 further trials across 26 models. Three of the four frontier models fall within 0.031 of one another (0.785 to 0.816) with no difference between them resolved, while the fourth scores 0.707 and all three gaps to it exclude zero. Three of the four do better on metadata lookup than on numeric calculation. The fourth is slightly better on numeric. Numeric tasks are 28 of the 131 but half of the twelve tasks that all four models fail. The ranking also depends on the evaluation budget: with one run per task, 23.9% of bootstrap replicates put a different model first. On a selected 15-task slice, removing network access lowers scores more than blocking eight structural-database domains, but the two contrasts were graded in different passes and cannot be cleanly decomposed. Swapping in each model's own command-line agent changes scores by -0.071 to +0.086, a comparison too small to rule out moderate harness effects. Across 26 models, numeric performance rises with non-numeric performance rather than staying flat. The experiments use different task subsets, so they cannot rank model, harness, access and task composition against one another. Evaluations should report results by task family, along with the number of runs, the harness and the access conditions.

title: What Language Adds, and at What Cost: Four Controlled Probes of Pathology Vision-Language Models
abstract: Vision--language models (VLMs) promise to make computational pathology queryable and able to draft reports, but how much language adds beyond the vision backbone is unclear, because almost every system is evaluated by its developers on test sets of their own choosing. We grade published evidence by how it was produced and test four claims with controlled probes that reuse released checkpoints and public data, varying one input at a time. Report text adds prognostic signal: adding a frozen embedding of the stage-redacted report to a slide embedding raises the pooled C-index by 0.019 for progression-free interval and by 0.016 for overall survival across 1{,}633 TCGA patients, and restoring the stage statement adds nothing. Prompts add no measurable accuracy at inference: with features and pooling fixed, zero-shot classification is statistically indistinguishable from a supervised linear probe for lung and renal cancer subtyping. Slide-level question answering is barely grounded: SlideChat answers 74.82\% of SlideBench-VQA(TCGA) items correctly with the slide and 74.41\% without it, whereas its language backbone alone reaches 43.52\%. Paraphrasing leaves accuracy unchanged but flips 8--23\% of answers. Self-reported gains from agentic navigation and few-shot language priors cannot yet be attributed to language. Language thus adds real but narrow value, and we propose minimum controls that would expose these failure modes in future evaluations.

title: DoAtlas-2: A Foundation for Self-Evolving Causal Biomedical Discovery
abstract: We introduce DoAtlas-2, a foundation for self-evolving causal biomedical discovery that organizes knowledge around causal mechanisms and advances through external evidence from human populations. DoAtlas-2 integrates 771 research resources covering more than 720,000 participants in 48 countries, from longitudinal clinical phenotypes, medical imaging, and continuous physiological signals to eight molecular layers, together with an evidence network of approximately 4.7 million literature-derived records over 93,566 concepts and 149,383 candidate causal relations. DoAtlas-2 autonomously formulates research questions from evidence gaps and unresolved mechanisms, prespecifies their causal designs, and generates validated analyses. Supporting, challenging, and unresolved results continuously revise mechanistic interpretations, the causal evidence state, and the discovery frontier, so that DoAtlas-2 self-evolves within a closed loop of hypothesis generation, empirical testing, and renewed discovery. DoAtlas-2 has systematically evaluated 2,031 research questions. In the Human Phenotype Project (HPP), it formulated 4,014 candidate pathway questions across vascular, early-glycemic, and hepatic-metabolic systems, and screening of the first 1,079 yielded statistical support for 756. Representative studies identify blood pressure as a convergence node linking adiposity, hepatic, and lipid phenotypes to vascular outcomes, and show that an adiposity-inflammation-blood-pressure pathway is largely attenuated by joint adjustment for body mass index (BMI) and smoking. The discovered vascular network constitutes a completely interpretable predictive foundation, admitting exact attribution of every prediction and closed-form mediation effects. DoAtlas-2 thereby unifies causal mechanism discovery, population-evidence testing, and interpretable prediction within one continuously evolving foundation.

title: Flow in a porous non-axisymmetric annular conduit: Coupling wall compliance and peristalsis
abstract: Coenen \textit{et al.}\ (\textit{J. Fluid Mech.}, vol.~921, 2021, p.~R2) developed a reduced-order model of peristaltic pumping in non-axisymmetric annular conduits with rigid walls, in the context of periarterial space (PAS) flows. \textit{In vivo} studies show that the PAS's outer wall undergoes significant displacement due to flow within and that the penetrating PASs form a porous pathway. To account for these biomechanical aspects, we revisit the problem of flow in an eccentric annular conduit and incorporate porous drag and two-way-coupled fluid--structure interaction between the compliant outer wall and the cerebrospinal fluid flow within. A Darcy--Brinkman term in the axial momentum equation accounts for drag due to the porous medium. We account for changes in hydraulic resistance due to peristalsis and compliant-wall displacements perturbatively, thereby reducing the problem to a single nonlinear partial differential equation for the axial pressure. This reduced-order model allows us to build a mechanistic understanding of flow through a porous penetrating PAS and enables parametric studies. For small-amplitude peristaltic waves, analytical solutions are possible.

title: Direct RNA sequence design under codon constraints using expressive tensor-based secondary structure models
abstract: Nucleic acid sequence design via codon optimization is a fundamental task with applications across synthetic biology, mRNA therapeutics, and vaccine design. Given a target protein, it is a major open challenge to navigate the combinatorially large design space of codon sequences mapping to its amino acid sequence. Computational approaches generally seek to optimize simple objectives based on the codon sequence, possibly together with more complicated contributions based on secondary structure analysis. In this work, we demonstrate a direct and efficient algorithm to sample sequences from a suitable Boltzmann distribution defined in terms of the codon sequence and a fully detailed secondary structure free energy model, as well as related algorithms for exact computation of statistical quantities such as free energies, base pairing probabilities, and base and codon marginals. These algorithms draw upon a recently developed tensor-based formulation of secondary structure thermodynamics and demonstrate, for the first time, that global sequence design can be accomplished with respect to a highly accurate free energy model. Moreover, the algorithms can leverage any available CPU and GPU resources in parallel for massive computational speedups.

title: Sensitivity and Identifiability of Tumor-Related Changes in Longitudinal Microwave Breast Imaging
abstract: Microwave imaging could monitor breast tumor response to neoadjuvant chemotherapy, but between-visit changes in breast positioning and normal tissue may confound tumor-related changes. We use eight patient-specific dielectric models from longitudinal MRI of two patients at four time points. For each model, 24-port S-parameters were simulated from 1 to 3 GHz, and Jacobians computed for tumor permittivity and loss, fibroglandular tissue (FGT) permittivity, and breast rotation and translation. 1 mm positioning changes produced changes 20 to 50 times larger than a 10% tumor permittivity change above 2 GHz. Nevertheless, tumor sensitivity patterns were weakly aligned with positioning patterns, tumor-FGT similarity exceeded 0.8 at only some visits, and the Jacobians remained well conditioned. Tumor responses are thus small but separable; monitoring will require positioning correction, frequency selection, and noise-aware detectability analysis.

title: Bombadil: A Foundation Model for Plant Electrophysiology
abstract: Living plants, like animals, use electrical signals to carry information about their physiological state across their body, from roots to branches. These signals can be recorded, as they are in animals, from a pair of differential extracellular electrodes inserted into signal-conducting tissue. While machine-learning models have been trained to predict specific plant stress states from these signals, each of these models has been trained for only a single task and none have been designed to transfer across tasks, species, or environments. These approaches do not allow easy scaling across the wide range of species and environments that are relevant to agriculture, forestry, and horticulture for both commercial and consumer plant care. Here we present Bombadil, a foundation model for plant electrophysiology, pretrained without labels on over 4 million hours of electrical signals recorded from 100 plant species in ten distinct environments, including laboratories, greenhouses, commercial orchards, and natural forests. In this way, Bombadil is able to learn the fundamental features of plant electrical signals across a wide array of species and environments. Then, from those same electrical signals, Bombadil tracks changes in seven physiological indicators of plant stress, even among species and stressors with no labels in training.

title: An Open-Source Web-Based Viewer for Disseminating Image-Derived Models
abstract: Patient-specific 3-dimensional (3D) models are increasingly central to planning surgery and catheter-based intervention in children with congenital heart disease (CHD), whose anatomy is often atypical and variable. These models inform care only when the surgeons and interventional cardiologists who make treatment decisions can rotate, crop, and measure them directly. Desktop modeling applications require local installation, capable hardware, and training. Commercial web-based viewers are portable but closed, and, in our experience, cannot display volume rendering, time-resolved (e.g., 4-dimensional) data, or the custom workflows centers build for CHD. Because CHD populations are small and heterogeneous, such workflows are unlikely to be prioritized commercially, and end users have no means to add them. To address these limitations, we developed the SlicerHeart Viewer, an open-source module that presents a simplified interface to a complete 3D Slicer/SlicerHeart session running on a server. Clinicians access models created by clinical modeling services from any device through a web browser. Because 3D Slicer runs underneath, volume rendering, time-resolved data, and any SlicerHeart workflow, including those developed for CHD, are available without modification. The module is independent of the hosting environment; we chose internal servers behind institutional single sign-on, and a cloud-hosted option is in development. Over one year at a single pediatric center, nearly all of 82 modeled cases were shared through the Viewer with clinicians from five specialties, with cases loading in 5 to 10 seconds. The approach is not specific to CHD and is deployable at other centers.

title: Three-dimensional stochastic retinal models for synthetic eye-models
abstract: Purpose: Current eye models often assume a fixed spherical retinal curvature of 12 mm, which does not reflect the anatomical variability observed in vivo. This study proposes an extension incorporating the stochastic relationship between axial length and three-dimensional (3D) retinal curvature, enabling more realistic 3D eye models. Methods: Axial length and 3D retinal curvature data from 94 subjects, split into five subsets for cross-validation, were used to construct two probabilistic models: a Single Gaussian Model (SGM) and two-component Multi Gaussian Mixture Model (MGMM). Both were converted into conditional forms to estimate retinal curvature for a specific axial length, and evaluated against measured data distributions. Results: All models produced radii of curvature comparable to measured data (median difference <0.2 mm). Non-conditionally, the MGMM described the distribution slightly better than SGM, with higher density overlap (>94% vs. >86%), but similar variance (worst f-test (p-value) 1.05 (0.71) vs. 1.05 (0.73)). Conditioned on axial length, both models performed similarly with overlap exceeding 93% and the worst f-test 1.02 (0.84). Given its simplicity and robustness, the conditional SGM was selected, achieving similar validation results: median difference (<0.10 mm), overlap (>92%), and a non-significant worst f-test (1.02 (0.85)). Conclusions: The conditional SGM enables accurate generation of anatomically realistic 3D retinal curvatures based on axial length, supporting improved stochastic eye modeling for visual optics and population-based simulations of healthy eyes. Translational relevance: Replacing the fixed 12 mm retina assumption with a population-based stochastic model improves anatomical accuracy of eye models used in optical design and treatment planning.

title: QProtFuse: Query-Guided Layer Fusion for Retrieval-Augmented Protein Function Prediction
abstract: Predicting protein functions from amino acid sequences is essential to understanding biological processes. Large language models (LLMs) offer flexible function descriptions to natural-language queries, yet their limited protein understanding motivates retrieval-augmented generation (RAG). Existing protein RAG methods primarily expand external retrieval signals while overlooking the rich knowledge encoded within a single protein language model (PLM). We show that retrieval performance varies across PLM layers and biological tasks, making conventional final-layer selection suboptimal. To this end, we propose QProtFuse, which uses queries to adaptively fuse multi-layer protein features and jointly learns protein and annotation retrieval through intra-modal and cross-modal contrastive objectives. On Prot-Inst-OOD, QProtFuse achieves the best protein and annotation retrieval scores, reaching 16.4\% Recall@1 with annotation reranking. These gains improve downstream RAG-based function descriptions, yielding the highest LLM-as-a-judge scores for both Qwen3-8B (6.22/10) and DeepSeek-V4-Pro (6.68/10). Ablations and weight analyses demonstrate the value of query-guided fusion and complementary training objectives for exploiting a PLM's internal knowledge.

title: Propensity Straight-Through Gradients for Discrete Stochastic Systems
abstract: We introduce the propensity straight-through (PST) estimator for gradient-based learning through exact simulations of continuous-time Markov chains (CTMCs). These models describe discrete stochastic dynamics across physics, chemistry, and biology, but their categorical event choices prevent ordinary differentiation. PST preserves exact forward trajectories and differentiates, in the backward pass, the normalized reaction propensities the simulator already computes. The affine state update makes this rule exact for the one-step conditional-mean sensitivity. We derive the per-step discrepancy for one-step sensitivities composed along nonlinear trajectories in closed form, show that it vanishes for affine downstream dependence, and bound it quadratically in the stoichiometric jump size. Across reversible dimerization, a genetic oscillator, a 50-task repressilator suite, and experimental patch-clamp recordings, PST recovers parameters to within 0.06-1.7% and converges 2.4-3.0-fold faster than the Gumbel-Softmax straight-through estimator at matched computational cost. At deep-learning scale, PST trains all 203,796 parameters of a stochastic reaction network using exact discrete events from initialization. By differentiating an exact conditional mean, PST eliminates reaction-selection temperature tuning and provides a scalable route to learning through exact stochastic dynamics.

title: Simulation-free approximate Bayesian computation for stochastic reaction networks
abstract: Uncovering stochastic reaction networks from data is central to single-cell biology. Simulation-based inference has evolved into a flexible paradigm for this purpose, circumventing the computational intractability of the likelihood. Notably, approximate Bayesian computation performs this inference by carrying out extensive Gillespie simulations, usually at a high computational cost. Here, we propose a simulation-free approximate Bayesian computation (SFABC) framework that avoids both simulation and explicit likelihood solutions of the network dynamics. Instead, SFABC exploits the Chemical Master Equation to formulate a tractable convex optimization with ensuing constraints, which are then used to accept sampled parameters consistent with the observed data. The resulting posterior approximation comes with theoretical guarantees: it can be tightened systematically, and it provably converges to the exact Bayesian posterior distributions. Using synthetic benchmarks, we show that SFABC matches the accuracy of standard simulation-based algorithms at a substantially reduced computational cost. We then showcase the applicability of SFABC to experimental systems biology by analyzing gene transcription bursting kinetics from snapshot, time-resolved, and cell-cycle-resolved single-cell data.

title: PyGPLA: A Python Package for Generalized Phase Locking Analysis
abstract: Spike-field couplings measure the links between neuronal spiking and local field potential (LFP) and provide a tool to study how neural populations coordinate activity across spatial and temporal scales. While modern high-density electrophysiology enables the simultaneous recording of numerous LFP channels and neuronal units, this massive scale poses significant statistical and computational challenges for conventional pairwise coupling analyses. The number of channel-unit comparisons grows rapidly, and a coherent population-level structure can be obscured by high-dimensional coupling matrices. Generalized Phase Locking Analysis (GPLA) addresses this challenge by organizing spike-triggered LFP phase information into a complex coupling matrix and extracting dominant low-rank modes. These modes summarize whether a population is coupled to the field, which channels and units contribute to the coupling, and how their relative phases are organized. Here, we present PyGPLA, an open-source Python package implementing GPLA for high-density electrophysiological recordings. Designed for straightforward integration into existing neural data analysis pipelines, PyGPLA supports multivariate spike-LFP coupling analysis, from coupling estimation and interpretation to significance assessment using analytical and surrogate-based tests.

title: Data-driven multi-agent modelling of calcium interactions in cell culture: PINN vs Regularized Least-squares
abstract: Data-driven discovery of dynamics in biological systems allows for better observation and characterization of processes, such as calcium signaling in cell culture. Recent advancements in techniques allow the exploration of previously unattainable insights of dynamical systems, such as the Sparse Identification of Non-Linear Dynamics (SINDy), overcoming the limitations of more classic methodologies. The latter requires some prior knowledge of an effective library of candidate terms, which is not realistic for a real case study. Using inspiration from fields like traffic density estimation and control theory, we propose a methodology for characterization and performance analysis of calcium delivery in a family of cells. In this work, we compare the performance of the Constrained Regularized Least-Squares Method (CRLSM) and Physics-Informed Neural Networks (PINN) for system identification and parameter discovery for governing ordinary differential equations (ODEs). The CRLSM achieves a fairly good parameter estimate and a good data fit when using the learned parameters in the Consensus problem. On the other hand, despite the initial hypothesis, PINNs fail to match the CRLSM performance and, under the current configuration, do not provide fair parameter estimation. However, we have only studied a limited number of PINN architectures, and it is expected that additional hyperparameter tuning, as well as uncertainty quantification, could significantly improve the performance in future works.

title: How Robust Are Prognostic Radiomic Features? Comparing Selection Techniques on Pooled Glioblastoma Cohorts
abstract: Radiomic survival studies in glioblastoma report heterogeneous prognostic features, but how much of this stems from the methodology itself is rarely examined. We analysed the association of 463 radiomic, anatomical and clinical features from pre-treatment MRI with overall survival in 705 IDH-wildtype glioblastoma patients from three public cohorts, using three techniques: a log-rank test after median split, univariate Cox regression (both Benjamini-Hochberg corrected) and an XGBoost regressor interpreted with SHAP. The log-rank test selected 99 features, Cox regression 72 and SHAP its top 20; five were selected by all three: age, a peritumoural T2 texture feature, the number of connected peritumoural mask components and two image-level intensity maxima. The two survival tests shared 51 features, about half of the SHAP top 20 were also selected by either test, and where selections overlapped, effect directions agreed. Many selections were PyRadiomics diagnostic descriptors that are not restricted to tumour voxels. Analytical pipeline choices, including ranking method, pre-filtering and descriptor handling, can substantially influence which features appear prognostic.

title: Application of Single-cell Deep Learning in Elucidating the Mapping Relationship Between Visceral and Body Surface Inflammatory Patterns
abstract: The subcutaneous fascia (scFascia) is a widely distributed connective tissue, yet its contribution to systemic responses during visceral inflammation remains insufficiently defined. In the rat model of Salmonella-induced dysentery, scRNA-seq of scFascia combined with deep neural network (DNN)-based nonlinear feature discovery revealed transcriptional alterations indicative of Warburg-like reprogramming in macrophages (MPs), accompanied by reduced activity of the citrate cycle. CD34+/PDGFRα+ telocytes (CPTCs) regulated MP differentiation and proliferation through Wnt/Fgf signaling, suggesting a pathological communication pattern between scFascia and visceral organs, termed the fascia-visceral inflammatory crosstalk pattern (FVICP). PySCENIC analysis showed increased activity of transcription factors Fosl1, Nfkb2, and Atf4, modulated by CPTC signaling to MPs, leading to downregulation of aerobic respiration and upregulation of the cell cycle, DNA replication, and transcription. Co-culture assays demonstrated that CPTCs suppressed the pro-inflammatory activity of MPs by transcriptionally downregulating TLR4 and CPT1A while upregulating ATF4, and enhanced anti-inflammatory potential via post-transcriptional MTOR upregulation. These findings highlight the role of scFascia in immunomodulation and metabolic reprogramming during visceral inflammation, emphasizing its contribution to systemic homeostasis.

title: evaluating local viscoelastic properties of artery-mimicking phantoms using high-resolution flexural wavenumber analysis
abstract: The measurement of guided wave propagation is an effective approach for evaluating arterial wall stiffness. A more comprehensive characterization of viscoelastic material properties could yield more informative biomarkers; however, this additionally requires estimation of wave attenuation. Furthermore, spatially local estimation is necessary for localized pathologies, such as atherosclerotic plaques. To this end, we propose an original two-stage high-resolution method to recover local viscoelastic properties from guided waves in artery-like soft tubes. First, the local frequency-wavenumber dispersion relation including losses is estimated using a high-resolution complex wavenumber identification method. Second, assuming a fractional Kelvin-Voigt rheological model for the tube wall, we estimate the viscoelastic material parameters by fitting the dispersion relation computed with a spectral element method to this estimate. We experimentally validate the proposed approach on flexural wave propagation along water-filled soft tubes, measured with a high-speed camera coupled with digital image correlation. Owing to the high resolution of the method, the axial modulus variation of a graded phantom is recovered. Finally, a Cramér-Rao analysis indicates that the complex wavenumber estimator operates near its theoretical limit, and reveals why local attenuation is intrinsically difficult to recover.

title: CPTCs Drive Somatic-Visceral Communication via the Wnt Axis in Somatic Mechanotherapy: A Single-Cell Deep Learning Study
abstract: Somatic mechanical stimulation (e.g., acupuncture) exerts systemic immunomodulatory effects, yet the cellular bridge translating peripheral physical force into visceral repair remains elusive. Here, employing a custom interpretable deep learning framework (CARSS) on single-cell RNA sequencing data, we identify CD34+PDGFRα+ telocytes (CPTCs) as the primary mechanosensors in both fascia and colon during bacterial colitis. We show that somatic mechanotherapy triggers an AP-1/Hsp70-dependent transcriptional program in fascial CPTCs, inducing systemic Wnt elevation, which elicits a "transcriptional resonance" in colonic CPTCs, reprogramming their communication network from an inflammatory amplifier to a Wnt-driven regenerative hub. Mechanistically, this axis activates epithelial \b{eta}-catenin/Myc signaling, suppressing apoptosis and restoring barrier integrity independent of immune cells. Our findings define a CPTC-Driven Mechano-Resonance Axis, where CPTCs serve as synchronized relay stations that convert somatic mechanical stimulation into systemic regenerative microenvironments.

title: Accurate quantification of protein concentrations and state populations by 2D 1H-N Q-BEST NMR
abstract: We introduce 2D Q-BEST NMR as a quantitative approach for determining protein concentrations and relative state populations from a set of three 1 H-15 N correlation spectra. The BEST methodology ensures short overall experimental times and highest sensitivity. The method was validated using ubiquitin as a model system, where a precision of approximately 15-20% was achieved at the level of individual cross-peaks. This precision can be further improved by averaging corrected intensities of well-resolved resonances corresponding to the same protein state. The approach was subsequently applied to the quantification of protein concentrations across multiple samples and to the determination of conformational state populations in proteins exhibiting intrinsic or ligand-induced heterogeneity. In both cases, 2D Q-BEST NMR provides accurate and robust quantification of NMR-visible species, demonstrating its utility as a general spectroscopic tool for quantitative biomolecular NMR analysis.

title: RNAGenScape: Property-Guided, Optimized Generation of mRNA Sequences with Manifold Langevin Dynamics
abstract: Generating property-optimized mRNA sequences is central to applications such as vaccine design and protein replacement therapy, but remains challenging due to limited data, complex sequence-function relationships, and the narrow space of biologically viable sequences. Generative methods that drift away from the data manifold can yield sequences that fail to fold, translate poorly, or are otherwise nonfunctional. We present RNAGenScape, a property-guided manifold Langevin dynamics framework for mRNA sequence generation that operates on a learned manifold of real data. By performing iterative local optimization constrained to this manifold, RNAGenScape preserves favorable computational viability proxies, accesses reliable guidance, and discourages excursions into regions poorly supported by the training data. The framework integrates three components: (1) an autoencoder jointly trained with a property predictor to learn a property-organized latent manifold, (2) a denoising autoencoder that projects updates back onto the manifold, and (3) a property-guided Langevin dynamics procedure that performs optimization along the manifold. Across three real-world mRNA datasets spanning two orders of magnitude in size, RNAGenScape increases median oracle-predicted property gain by up to 267% and success rate by up to 31%, while maintaining good biological viability proxy measures and achieving competitive inference efficiency compared to existing generative approaches.

title: HyperTaxa: Multiscale Genome Representations for Generalized Microbial Taxonomic Inference
abstract: Reliable microbial taxonomic inference is challenged by the rapid growth of newly sequenced organisms and incomplete reference coverage. While alignment- and database-driven tools remain essential for reference-backed identification, they are not designed for learned inference over species absent from genome-level training. We introduce HyperTaxa, a taxonomy-aligned representation learning framework for open-set microbial taxonomic inference. HyperTaxa encodes whole genomes as multiscale hyperspectral k-mer transition fields and aligns these representations to a taxonomy-derived semantic space using a two-stage Node2Vec-to-MDS procedure that combines local graph structure with global hierarchical distance preservation. The resulting space supports zero-shot inference over species excluded from genome-level training but represented in the taxonomy, generalized zero-shot inference over seen and unseen species, and cascaded genus-to-species prediction. Across benchmark and large-scale disjoint-species evaluations, HyperTaxa improves taxonomic prediction over pseudo-image and transformer-graph baselines, with the strongest gains at higher taxonomic ranks. Ablations further show that multiscale transition encoding and taxonomy-aware alignment are key contributors to generalization. These results position HyperTaxa as a complementary taxonomy-aware representation and candidate-generation framework for microbial identification under incomplete reference coverage and open-set uncertainty.

title: Evaluating Conformal Reliability of Pathway-Level Transcriptomic Signatures Under Cross-Cohort Shift in Sepsis Mortality Prediction
abstract: Blood transcriptomic profiling enables prognostic modeling by capturing the host immune response at the molecular level. Yet, the within-cohort evaluation strategies employed by many transcriptomic models inadequately reflect deployment across independent hospitals. Outside deployment scenarios introduce a cohort shift that can substantially degrade predictive performance and reliability of uncertainty estimates. We present a framework for evaluating transcriptomic sepsis mortality prediction under realistic cross-cohort deployment, systematically comparing gene-level, pathway-level and hybrid molecular representations. Four publicly available whole-blood transcriptomic cohorts consisting of 936 patients and 248 mortality events were harmonized into a shared 7,660-gene feature space and evaluated under leave-one-cohort-out validation using logistic regression, random forests, XGBoost and LightGBM. Beyond AUROC and AUPRC, model behavior was evaluated via conformal prediction, calibration analysis, selective prediction and the proposed Pathway Stability Index. Gene-level and hybrid representations were found to generally achieve the strongest discriminative performance, whereas pathway-level representations exhibited greater robustness across model families, more reliable uncertainty behavior under cross-cohort shift and stable molecular signatures enriched for immune and host-defense processes identified through Gene Ontology and KEGG enrichment analyses. These findings demonstrate that molecular representation influences not only predictive discrimination but also calibration, uncertainty reliability, biological coherence and transferability under external validation.

title: Harmonic Torsional Diffusion for Protein-Ligand Flexible Docking
abstract: Molecular docking requires reasoning jointly about ligand pose and protein flexibility. Most diffusion-based docking models predict torsional updates with generic Euclidean heads that ignore the periodic geometry of angular variables. This mismatch is especially limiting in flexible docking, where ligand conformations and pocket side chains co-adapt to form the bound complex. Here, we introduce Harmony, a harmonic torsional diffusion framework for flexible protein-ligand docking. Harmony parameterizes ligand and side-chain torsional score fields as derivatives of learned harmonic potentials on the circle, which are noised mode by mode in the Fourier basis owing to the properties of variance-exploding diffusion on the torus. This construction makes periodicity explicit and gives the model a frequency-aware inductive bias over rotameric motion. On the PDBBind benchmark, Harmony improves ligand pose accuracy and pocket all-atom reconstruction over recent flexible docking methods. On PoseBusters, it improves the physical validity of generated complexes. Case studies on EBNA1 and KRAS G12D illustrate the method's behavior on a polar and a shallow binding site, respectively. Together, these results indicate that aligning the score parameterization with the geometry of the diffusion process is a simple and effective lever for improving flexible docking.

title: panvram: GPU-resident random access to a human pangenome cohort
abstract: Repeatedly sampling short sequence windows from a human pangenome requires an access representation as well as compression. panvram stores each assembly as a reference-relative block archive and pools these archives on a GPU. For 558 haplotype assemblies, the default q4k representation occupies 16.642 GB of persistent pools including the decoded reference; a packed-reference, compact-directory representation occupies 11.634 GB. These quantities are not peak application memory. In the C1 experiment, default and fully compact forms delivered 743,271 and 736,762 windows/s; a separate public Colab run delivered 741,931 and 680,760 windows/s. All are batch API measurements and must not be pooled as repeated trials of an identical environment. Full-decoding checks compared reconstructed FASTA checksums with the manifest. On the CPU, the M6 shuffled-window workload at the same cohort cardinality reported 26 requests/s for AGC and 145,222 requests/s for refrel3 q4k. This comparison concerns one-thread requests of 4 KiB on the recorded warm-cache workload, not all genome-access patterns. AGC provides the smaller incremental archive: 5.40 MB/assembly versus 13.04 MB/assembly for refrel3 q16k, with different exclusions; the size pair is not the same refrel3 configuration as the q4k timing pair. We derive an expected-work expression for fixed independent granules and distinguish it from an empirical median-latency predictor. Cohort-scale counter and DRAM measurements motivate a locality hypothesis, but do not establish a causal per-miss latency or independently reproduce a model-failure verdict. The window-cost verdict at N=558 is published with its harness and raw timings.

title: Spontaneous brain-wide rotational dynamics constrain cue-evoked behavior
abstract: Uncovering low-dimensional representations of brain-wide neural dynamics and their relationship to behavior remains a central challenge. Here, we show that spontaneous brain-wide rotational dynamics constrain cue-evoked behavior and learning. To systematically establish these findings, we developed a dimensionality-reduction technique called Rotational Component Analysis (RCA) that optimizes the detection of low-variance rotational modes even within individual trials. We applied RCA to motor-cortical spike-train data from monkeys and humans, mouse cortex-wide calcium imaging, and human functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) and magnetoencephalography (MEG). In mice, a rotational mode identified from activity recorded at rest predicts cue-evoked behavior: the phase of rotation when a randomly timed cue arrives predicts whether the animal subsequently pulls the lever. We explain this surprisingly strong correlation using both a recurrent neural network (RNN) and a minimal two-dimensional model of response learning, in which the intrinsic rotational mode serves as a dynamical constraint on response and learning. We further identify double-rotation modes containing two centers of rotation that separate preparatory from task dynamics in both mouse and human data. Remarkably, corresponding modes also organize neural dynamics during a non-motor human task, and rotational irreversibility captures early psychosis even when principal component analysis shows no group difference. Our work establishes rotational dynamics as low-dimensional coordinates that constrain how ongoing brain states are converted into behavior. More broadly, RCA provides a versatile tool for detecting hidden nonreciprocal dynamics in biological and physical datasets.

title: Double-Take: Improving Capacity, Binding, and Selectivity In Long-Context Within Bidirectional Memory
abstract: Processing a long sequence does not guarantee that distant information remains usable. As context grows, a fixed-size memory must retain many associations, connect information across positions, and preserve relevant structure without being overwhelmed by everything it observes. These are distinct requirements: a memory may store more information without representing the relationships needed for retrieval, and it may transport those relationships without preserving the ones that matter. Thus, the challenge is not simply extending context length, but constructing a memory that remains usable as context grows. We study this problem in large-chunk test-time training (TTT) and identify two basic failures: single-step writes accumulate interference, limiting capacity, while self-associative writes cannot form cross-position bindings. We introduce Double-Take (DT), which repairs these failures with multi-step unpinned updates and cross-position mixing, and adds bidirectional change-sensitive writes for selective retention. Capacity alone leaves end-to-end recall at the $0.10$ chance floor; adding binding raises it to $0.92$. Trained only on $32\,\mathrm{kb}$ genomic contexts, DT reaches $0.927$ AUROC at $131\,\mathrm{kb}$ and $0.856$ near $1\,\mathrm{Mb}$, while transferring zero-shot from human to mouse. Together, these results identify capacity, binding, and selectivity as three requirements for usable long-range memory.

title: Label-Space Mismatch Distorts Cross-Cohort Evaluation in Breast Cancer Molecular Subtyping
abstract: Cross-cohort evaluation of breast cancer subtype classifiers is unreliable when source and target cohorts use different annotation standards: METABRIC labels six classes, PAM50 defines five, and a claudin-low prediction cannot be correct under a five-class standard. A classifier transferred from 1,369 METABRIC patients (train n=958) to TCGA-BRCA (n=987) and GSE21653 (n=266) separates three evaluation operations routinely conflated in cross-site comparisons. (1) Label-space restriction - an evaluation-rule change, not a retraining gain - is the dominant correction (73.76%->79.74% on TCGA-BRCA; 63.16%->68.42% on GSE21653); (2) EM prior correction on the reconciled space is an optional calibration step (Brier fidelity up, macro F1 down; to 80.65% and 74.06%); and (3) the target label space is not recoverable from unlabelled predictions (EM retains prior 0.0751 on the absent class; calibrated detectors fail), so compliance must come from cohort documentation. The protocol exposes why internal validation overstates cross-cohort value: multimodal fusion gains do not transfer (no configuration beats mRNA alone, n=694; McNemar p=0.13-1.00), and the genomic panel adds nothing to pathological complete response prediction over clinical variables (DeltaAUC = +0.0045). Clinically, without label-space compliance, cross-site accuracy comparisons misattribute annotation-standard differences to model skill; Luminal A/B and claudin-low boundary errors map to distinct treatment decisions; and subtype accuracy is a weaker portable endpoint than survival discrimination (external C-index 0.577-0.584). Reporting the cohort's allowed label set and applying label-space compliance are therefore prerequisites before any cross-cohort performance claim.

title: Hybrid Context Forests and Bilateral Viterbi Matching for 3D Rib Centerline Tracing in CT
abstract: Automatic extraction and anatomical numbering (R01-R12, L01-L12) of all 24 rib centerlines in thoracic CT is essential for unfolded rib visualization, fracture detection, and surgical navigation, but remains challenging due to adjacent-bone confluence, calcified costal cartilage bridges, kyphotic pose variation, and partial visibility of terminal ribs. We present ribline, an open-source three-stage framework combining: (1) an automatically detected lung-apex and vertebral-midline coordinate frame with a kyphosis-aware azimuthal angle for point ordering along each rib; (2) a hybrid voxel detector fusing an anatomically anchored Semantic Context Forest (SCF) with a lightweight 3D U-Net; and (3) a global stage that decomposes the probability skeleton into candidate curves, assigns rib indices via a bilateral Viterbi dynamic program coupled across both hemithoraces, and refines curves via template recovery and normal-plane centering (RibSnake). On the Siemens Corporate Research 2 mm thoracic CT benchmark (47 training and 12 evaluation scans), our pipeline achieves a labeled Chamfer distance of 2.05 mm, labeled clDice of 0.886 (3 mm) and 0.945 (4 mm), 97.2% labeling accuracy (278/286 ribs), and zero false-positive curves on the evaluation split, and 3.64 mm (median 2.39 mm) with 91.8% labeling accuracy across all 59 annotated scans (1,402 ribs) in 5-fold cross-validation. title: Sensitive dependence of the motion of a legged robot on granular media
abstract: Legged locomotion on flowing ground ({\em e.g.} granular media) is unlike locomotion on hard ground because feet experience both solid- and fluid-like forces during surface penetration. Recent bio-inspired legged robots display speed relative to body size on hard ground comparable to high performing organisms like cockroaches but suffer significant performance loss on flowing materials like sand. In laboratory experiments we study the performance (speed) of a small (2.3 kg) six-legged robot, SandBot, as it runs on a bed of granular media (1 mm poppy seeds). For an alternating tripod gait on the granular bed, standard gait control parameters achieve speeds at best two orders of magnitude smaller than the 2 body lengths/s ($\approx 60$ cm/s) for motion on hard ground. However, empirical adjustment of these control parameters away from the hard ground settings, restores good performance, yielding top speeds of 30 cm/s. Robot speed depends sensitively on the packing fraction $φ$ and the limb frequency $ω$, and a dramatic transition from rotary walking to slow swimming occurs when $φ$ becomes small enough and/or $ω$ large enough. We propose a kinematic model of the rotary walking mode based on generic features of penetration and slip of a curved limb in granular media. The model captures the dependence of robot speed on limb frequency and the transition between walking and swimming modes but highlights the need for a deeper understanding of the physics of granular media.
journal_ref: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences (2009), 106 (9), 3029-3034

title: WILSON - Multi-magnification composites as a foundation for patient-level pathology analysis and diagnostic text generation
abstract: Pathologists examine tissue sections across multiple magnifications and slides, integrating morphological information to establish a diagnosis. In contrast, most pathology foundation models encode thousands of image patches from a single representative ("best") slide and aggregate their features, limiting multiscale and patient-level contextual integration. Here we introduce WILSON, a vision-language foundation model that represents whole-slide images and multi-slide cases through multi-magnification composites. Trained on approximately 189,000 slides spanning 42 organs and 838 diagnostic entities, WILSON enables patient-level analysis, multimodal retrieval and diagnostic text generation. Without task-specific training, WILSON outperformed a dedicated case-level model (macro-F1, 0.52 versus 0.38) and matched substantially larger slide-level models while requiring 400-1,350 times fewer computational operations. End-to-end fine-tuning improved breast cancer subtyping and stromal lymphocyte grading. WILSON also surpassed PRISM in image-text retrieval (recall@1, 75.6% versus 58.1%) and generated diagnostic descriptions that received higher ratings from five board-certified pathologists than competing models. These findings demonstrate that compact, multiscale representations can support computationally efficient, clinically grounded pathology foundation models.

title: SiLVi: Simple Interface for Labeling Video Interactions
abstract: Computer vision methods are increasingly used for the automated analysis of large volumes of video data collected through camera traps, drones, or direct observations of animals in the wild. While recent advances have focused primarily on detecting individual actions, much less work has addressed the detection and annotation of interactions -- a crucial aspect for understanding social and individualized animal behavior. Existing open-source annotation tools support either behavioral labeling without localization of individuals, or localization without the capacity to capture interactions. To bridge this gap, we present SiLVi, an open-source labeling software that integrates both functionalities. SiLVi enables researchers to annotate behaviors and interactions directly within video data, generating structured outputs suitable for training and validating computer vision models. By linking behavioral ecology with computer vision, SiLVi facilitates the development of automated approaches for fine-grained behavioral analyses. Although developed primarily in the context of animal behavior, SiLVi could be useful more broadly to annotate human interactions in other videos that require extracting dynamic scene graphs. The software, along with documentation and download instructions, is available at: https://silvi.ozankanbertay.com.

title: Quantifying Memorization and Privacy Risks in Genomic Language Models
abstract: Genomic language models (GLMs) have emerged as powerful tools for learning representations of DNA sequences, enabling advances in variant prediction, regulatory element identification, and cross-task transfer learning. However, as these models are increasingly trained or fine-tuned on sensitive genomic cohorts, they risk memorizing specific sequences from their training data, raising serious concerns around privacy, data leakage, and regulatory compliance. Despite growing awareness of memorization risks in general-purpose language models, little systematic evaluation exists for these risks in the genomic domain, where data exhibit unique properties such as a fixed nucleotide alphabet, strong biological structure, and individual identifiability. We present a comprehensive, multi-vector privacy evaluation framework designed to quantify memorization risks in GLMs. Our approach integrates three complementary risk assessment methodologies: perplexity-based detection, canary sequence extraction, and membership inference. These are combined into a unified evaluation pipeline that produces a worst-case memorization risk score. To enable controlled evaluation, we plant canary sequences at varying repetition rates into both synthetic and real genomic datasets, allowing precise quantification of how repetition and training dynamics influence memorization. We evaluate our framework across multiple GLM architectures, examining the relationship between sequence repetition, model capacity, and memorization risk. Our results establish that GLMs exhibit measurable memorization and that the degree of memorization varies across architectures and training regimes. These findings reveal that no single attack vector captures the full scope of memorization risk, underscoring the need for multi-vector privacy auditing as a standard practice for genomic AI systems.

title: Aptamers as a sandbox for lab-in-the-loop agentic molecular discovery
abstract: Despite breakthroughs in AI-driven molecular generation, existing discovery pipelines operate largely in silico, with wet-lab feedback reserved for validation rather than iterative improvement. Whether large language model (LLM)-based reasoning agents can accelerate de novo discovery by iterating with lab data remains unproven. Here we use protein-binding aptamer design as a sandbox (1-2 week cycles, \$1-\$3 per candidate) to demonstrate a wet lab in a closed loop with AI systems. We tasked agentic pipelines with developing aptamer binders against $α$-thrombin and myoglobin across three design-test-improve cycles ($\sim$1,000 candidates per round; $\sim$4,400 constructs). Statistically significant, bead-corrected on-target hit rates among new candidates rose across rounds from 0.0% in Round 1 to 26.0% in Round 2 and 42.1% in Round 3 on $α$-thrombin (37.1% excluding literature motif descendants), and from 10.2% in Round 1 to 3.7% in Round 2 and 33.5% in Round 3 on myoglobin. Single-clone bead-binding titrations of eight full-length $α$-thrombin candidates confirmed concordance with pooled sequencing enrichment (Pearson $r = 0.90$). In these assays, literature-derived motifs engineered by the agents to reduce off-target reactivity in the pooled screen reached apparent affinities of $K_D = 24.6$--$133$ nM, whereas de novo scaffolds showed low-micromolar binding ($K_D > 1\ μ$M). We also report how our pipelines used myoglobin binding data to exploit the G-quadruplex binder space, diagnose cross-reactivity as on-target specificity dropped from 75.0% to 19.1%, and recover by developing strategies that restored specificity to 72.4%. We demonstrate that empirical lab data is more valuable than existing computational proxies, showing how iterative experimental feedback enables AI agents to diagnose assay artifacts and refine molecular designs across rounds.

title: Evidence-informed dynamic modelling and intervention prioritisation in diabetic bone marrow
abstract: Aims. Fragmented understanding of how diabetes disrupts interconnected bone marrow niches has hindered integrated strategies to restore function. Building on a previous static network, we developed a dynamic model to simulate intervention responses. Methods. The investigator and ChatGPT dialogued to extract evidence from a frozen corpus and develop the model. A Python implementation extended Boolean logic to three ordinal levels (0, 1 and 2) representing biological states and, where applicable, intervention strength. Under high metabolic stress, 15 interventions were assessed at three strengths and four with binary settings; 171 pairs were tested at maximal strength. A domain balanced score (0 to100) integrated favourable and adverse changes. Staged simulations assessed withdrawal; regulatory constraints on recovery after metabolic stress reduction were examined separately. Results. Endothelial reactive oxygen species (ROS) suppression achieved the highest score among 19 single interventions (24.2), improving three functional domains. Endothelial protein kinase B (Akt) augmentation scored 15.2 (two domains); oncostatin M (OSM) blockade and haematopoietic 66 kDa SHC transforming protein 1 (p66Shc) loss each scored 13.6 (two domains). ROS suppression combined with either OSM blockade or p66Shc loss scored 37.9, (five domains). No pair restored all functions under high stress. Benefits of ROS suppression, Akt augmentation and ROS and OSM blockade disappeared after withdrawal. Reducing metabolic stress led to variable scores (range 4.5 to 100), increasing mainly with restored endothelial function, followed by progenitor recovery and interruption of inflammatory and adipocyte stromal signalling. Conclusions. These simulations offer a rule based framework for investigating diabetic marrow recovery. Experimental studies must establish whether it can guide targeted therapy.

title: Do Vision CIL Methods Transfer to Protein? A Diagnostic Benchmark of Frozen Protein Encoders
abstract: Protein function annotation operates over an expanding label space, making class-incremental learning (CIL) a natural framework for incorporating newly discovered functions without full retraining. Yet existing CIL methods have been developed largely in vision and have not been systematically evaluated over frozen protein representations. We conduct a controlled benchmark of nine representative CIL methods across five sequence-, structure-, and sequence--structure-based protein encoders and two enzyme function datasets at different scales, while keeping the encoders frozen and evaluation settings consistent across representations. We find that no method transfers reliably across encoders, and that these failures persist across alternative phase constructions. Diagnostic analyses reveal that this instability arises from weak gradient-based stability signals, substantial heterogeneity in embedding geometry, and covariance assumptions whose appropriate capacity changes with both dataset scale and encoder. These findings suggest that the representation itself should be treated as a central component of continual-learning design rather than a passive feature extractor. More generally, reliable protein CIL will require encoder-aware methods that adapt their statistical assumptions and capacity to the geometry of the representation on which they operate. Code is available at https://github.com/zygao930/ProteinCIL.

title: CADS: Measuring the Incremental Contribution of LLM Proposers in Sequential Biological Screens
abstract: Large language models are increasingly used to guide sequential biological screens, yet standard evaluations rely on raw hit counts that conflate a proposer's value with the discovery capacity of the underlying algorithmic harness. Adaptive sampling and corrupted experimental readouts also leave standard feedback comparisons without a false-discovery guarantee. We present Certified Agentic Discovery Screens (CADS), an error-controlled measurement framework that quantifies a proposer's incremental value against an identical LLM-free loop. By integrating capped likelihood-ratio bounds, e-processes, and complete-family e-BH, CADS controls the terminal false discovery rate under the stated null and corruption conditions despite arbitrary dependence, adaptive sampling, and optional stopping. In DepMap-backed simulations, CADS exposes two evaluation artifacts: the LLM-free harness alone clears the feedback gate, and raw origin counts overstate LLM contributions because LLM picks displace fallback discoveries. On the initial 20 seeds, supplying tested-candidate history to Qwen2.5-7B shifts its net contribution from +0.35, with a 95% interval covering zero, to +2.90, with the interval above zero. This initial net effect did not persist in a 50-seed matched-quota replication. These results support net gain over an LLM-free loop, measured between separately certified sets, as the appropriate measure of proposer contribution.

title: Global stability of Michaelis-Menten networks
abstract: In a very nice paper, Blanchini, Breda, Giordano and Liessi studied networks of species coupled through Michaelis-Menten interactions. Under standard assumptions of strong connectedness and non-degeneracy, they show that there is a unique equilibrium, which is (locally) asymptotically stable. This note shows that global stability, which was stated there as an open problem, holds as well. In fact, whenever a positive equilibrium exists, it attracts every solution with positive initial condition, with no connectedness or non-degeneracy hypothesis at all; those assumptions are needed only in order to guarantee existence and to cover solutions starting on the boundary of the orthant. The key is to note that the system is contractive with respect to the Thompson part metric.
